What a mature bioswale becomes

A living system for groundwater recharge, healthy soil, trees, habitat, mulch, and biodiversity.

A living water-harvesting ecosystem Rain is slowed, spread across the contour, absorbed through living soil, and cycled through roots, trees, wildlife, and groundwater.
The thin layer of soil that forms a patchy covering over the continents controls our own existence.
Rachel Carson · Silent Spring · 1962 Earthline uses Carson’s verified wording rather than repeating the unverified “two inches of soil” internet version.
A mature bioswale on a gentle slope Native trees, shrubs, flowers, mulch, fungi, insects, and deep roots turn a simple earthwork into long-term landscape resilience.
Once one has learned to harvest water, then the real fun begins.
Bill Mollison · Permaculture Lecture Series Water harvesting creates the foundation for productive soil, vegetation, habitat, groundwater support, and a cooler, more resilient landscape.
